Disgrace
dis-GRAYSS
v.t., n. (to bring shame or dishonor upon; the state of being out of favor; shame; dishonor)
Old French desgracier, from dis-, undoing, and Latin gratia, favor or grace. To disgrace is, at root, to remove someone or something from a state of grace or favor — the exact opposite motion the word grace itself names.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah's one use of the word belongs to a prayer of national lament, offered on behalf of a people under judgment who nonetheless dare to plead the LORD's own honor as their ground of appeal: Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory: remember, break not thy covenant with us. The petition is careful and theologically precise. It does not primarily ask for Israel's own comfort; it argues that Israel's continued desolation would itself disgrace the throne of the LORD's own glory, since His name and His covenant people had, by His own choosing, become bound together in the world's sight.

The logic depends entirely on covenant, not on any remaining merit in the people making the plea — the same chapter freely confesses that their iniquities testify against them and their backslidings are many. What the prayer appeals to instead is the LORD's own reputation, staked publicly on His covenant with this particular people; to disgrace them beyond recovery would be, in the terms the prayer itself supplies, to disgrace the throne from which He reigns. It is a bold form of intercession, arguing not from the petitioner's worthiness but from the petitioned One's own glory, and it stands as one model for prayer offered by a people who have no claim left except the name they were called by.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to bring shame or reproach upon; to dishonor; also, the state of being out of favor, or in a condition of shame.

expand to see more

DISGRACE, v.t. To bring reproach or shame upon; to dishonor; to treat with contempt or indignity.

ABHOR, v.t. To hate extremely; to detest; to regard with disgust and repugnance.

GLORY, n. Splendor; magnificence; honor and praise, especially as ascribed to God.

COVENANT, n. A solemn, binding agreement between parties, especially between God and his people.

INTERCESSION, n. The act of interceding; prayer or entreaty in favor of another, or on behalf of oneself before God.

Key Scripture

Jer 14:7 — "O LORD, though our iniquities testify against us, do thou it for thy name's sake: for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against thee."

Jer 14:21 — "Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory: remember, break not thy covenant with us."

Eze 36:22 — "Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; I do not this for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name's sake, which ye have profaned among the heathen, whither ye went."

Psa 79:9 — "Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake."

Modern Corruption

Prayer is treated as valid only when it appeals to the petitioner's own worthiness or need, when Jeremiah's boldest intercession appeals instead to the LORD's own glory and covenant name, staking nothing on Israel's merit at all.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; disgrace still names shame or dishonor. The principle worth recovering is the specific shape of covenant intercession Jeremiah models here. He does not minimize Israel's guilt, confessing in the very same prayer that their iniquities testify against them and their backslidings are many; and he does not, on that basis, abandon hope, because the prayer's real argument was never Israel's worthiness in the first place.

Ezekiel's later oracle states the same principle even more starkly from the LORD's own side: I do not this for your sakes... but for mine holy name's sake. A people bound to God by covenant can appeal to His own glory precisely because His name has been publicly attached to their fate; to let them be disgraced beyond recovery would, by the very terms of the covenant He established, touch the honor of the throne itself. This is not presumption but the specific, textured logic of a prayer that has nothing left to offer except the name it was called by.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew na'ats (H5006), to despise, to spurn; the verb behind “disgrace” in Jeremiah 14:21, elsewhere rendered abhor or blaspheme.

expand to see more

Hebrew na'ats (H5006) — to despise, spurn, disgrace; the verb rendered “disgrace” in Jeremiah 14:21, elsewhere translated abhor or provoke.

Hebrew kavod (H3519) — glory, honor, weight; the noun behind “the throne of thy glory,” the LORD's own honor bound up with His people's fate.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the binding agreement the prayer appeals to and asks not to be broken.

Hebrew chalal (H2490) — to profane, to defile; the verb behind Ezekiel 36:22's account of the LORD's name profaned among the nations.

Hebrew shem (H8034) — name; the covenant name at stake in every one of these prayers, the ground of the appeal rather than the petitioners' own merit.

Usage

"“do not disgrace the throne of thy glory” — Jeremiah's bold covenant appeal."

"“though our iniquities testify against us... do thou it for thy name's sake” — the confession the appeal is built on."

"“I do not this for your sakes... but for mine holy name's sake” — the LORD's own statement of the same principle."
